summary: Describes management and operational requirements for the address and routing parameter area domain, arpa, which is a special part of the DNS. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: It sets rules for running the special corner of the Internet phone book used for looking up addresses.

subtitle: The rules the IAB uses to run the special arpa domain that holds the DNS lookups Internet infrastructure depends on.

tldr.problem: The arpa domain supports DNS lookups such as reverse address mapping that many services rely on, so its management and operation need clear rules.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB, with ICANN, manages arpa as an infrastructure domain. Sub-domains are added only when an IETF Standards Track document describes them and recommends arpa in its IANA Considerations. The servers must meet the root server operational requirements of RFC 2870.
tldr.outcome: This is the Best Current Practice for how arpa is run. The text notes that it is updated by RFC 9120.

today: RFC 3172 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 52) and is updated by RFC 9120. Read the two together for the current rules.

sections.title: Why arpa Needs Management
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) mostly turns a structured text name into a protocol value, such as an IP address. It can also work the other way, turning protocol values into names of service entities. To do that, protocol values are transformed into a hierarchical name that serves as the lookup key.

The common example is reverse lookup of an IPv4 address. The address 128.9.160.55 is associated with the name www.iab.org. by creating the entry 55.160.9.128.in-addr.arpa. and mapping it, with a DNS PTR record, to that name. Applications depend on the correct and efficient operation of the arpa name servers, which is why RFC 3172 sets out management principles.
sections.eli5: Normally you look up a friend's name to find their phone number. Sometimes you have the number and want the name. The arpa domain is the part of the phone book built for that backwards lookup.

sections.title: What the arpa Domain Is
sections.content:
The arpa domain was set up at the start of DNS deployment, as a transition from the Host Tables common in the ARPANET and as a home for the IPv4 reverse mapping domain. During 2000, the abbreviation was redesignated "Address and Routing Parameter Area" to reduce confusion with the earlier network name.

It is called an infrastructure domain: its role is to support the operating infrastructure of the Internet. It provides a name root for mapping protocol values into lookup keys for operationally critical protocol data. It is explicitly not to be used like other generic top level domains, for example for naming hosts.

Appendix A reproduces an April 28, 2000 letter from the US Department of Commerce to ICANN. It records that DARPA signaled its disassociation with the domain on April 14, 2000, and asks ICANN to administer arpa under the guidance of the IAB as a limited use domain for Internet infrastructure applications.
sections.eli5: The name arpa used to be tied to an old network. It was kept but given a new meaning, so now it is just the street where the Internet's behind-the-scenes address books live.

sections.title: Who Runs arpa
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB), in cooperation with ICANN, is responsible for managing the arpa top level domain. The operational administration is performed by the IANA under the terms of the MoU between the IAB and ICANN concerning the IANA, which is RFC 2860.

The IAB decides which protocol elements are loaded into arpa and how they are structured. The job of managing a sub-domain may be delegated by the IAB to an appropriate protocol management entity. The IAB may add other infrastructure uses in the future, following the procedures in this document.
sections.eli5: One group decides what goes in the special phone book, and another group does the daily upkeep. They can also hand a chapter to a team that knows that subject best.

sections.title: Rules for Adding Sub-domains
sections.content:
Sub-domains of arpa are for protocol object sets defined as part of the Internet Standards Process. The IAB shall only recommend a sub-domain when two conditions hold. First, the delegation and the hierarchical name structure are described by an IETF Standards Track document. Second, that document's "IANA Considerations" section explicitly recommends using arpa.

That section should give the sub-domain name, the rules for administering it, and the criteria for entries. It should also say how protocol objects map to lookup keys. The IESG considers this section when it reviews the document. If the document is approved, the IESG asks the IAB to request that the IANA add the sub-domain.

Infrastructure domains located elsewhere in the DNS tree should follow the same requirements, and consideration should be given to migrating them into arpa when appropriate.
sections.eli5: You cannot just add a page to this phone book. A proper written standard must say what the page is and ask for it, and then the right committees approve it.

sections.title: Name Server Requirements
sections.content:
Because the domain is part of the operationally critical infrastructure, it is placed at the top level. This avoids the instability that would come from multiple DNS lookups across several operational domains to find the servers of a deeper nested infrastructure name. The maximal lookup is a query to a root server for the arpa name servers, which returns the list of authoritative arpa servers.

All operational requirements in RFC 2870 that apply to root servers also apply to the arpa servers, including any later revision of that RFC.

Many of the servers authoritative for the root zone also served the arpa zone at the time. The text, following RFC 2870, says this arrangement is likely to change.
sections.eli5: Because so much depends on this phone book, the people running its copies must follow the same strict rules as the keepers of the main Internet directory.

sections.title: The Sub-domains in Use
sections.content:
The RFC lists three sub-domains in use at the time: in-addr.arpa, ip6.arpa and e164.arpa.

in-addr.arpa is the IPv4 reverse address domain, delegated to the IANA, with sub-delegations made in line with IANA address allocation practices. ip6.arpa is the IPv6 reverse address domain, delegated the same way, with names further delegated to the regional IP registries following the delegation of IPv6 address space to them. e164.arpa maps E.164 telephone numbers into URIs, as defined in RFC 2916.

At the time of writing, the arpa zone sat on a subset of the root servers, and the IAB was working with ICANN, IANA and the regional registries to move arpa and in-addr.arpa records off the root servers, in line with the recommendation in RFC 2870 for exclusive use of those servers.
sections.eli5: Three chapters of the phone book exist: one for looking up old-style addresses, one for new-style addresses, and one for turning telephone numbers into Internet names.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2870, and any successors, apply to the operation of the arpa servers. The security considerations specific to the E.164 sub-domain are in Section 5 of RFC 2916. Any new sub-domain delegation must adequately document the security considerations specific to the information stored there.

For the IANA, the IAB may request delegation of arpa sub-domains in line with the IANA Considerations section of an IETF Standards Track document. This request falls under Section 4 of the MoU between the IETF and ICANN concerning the IANA.
sections.eli5: Anyone adding a new chapter has to explain how it could be abused and how to keep it safe, and the usual strict safety rules for the main directory also apply here.
